playground.label: Meal ingredients database: two linked tables (uses input)
playground.code:
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect(':memory:', autocommit=True)
conn.execute('PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON')
conn.execute('CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS meals (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE) STRICT')
conn.execute('CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ingredients (name TEXT NOT NULL, meal_id INTEGER NOT NULL, FOREIGN KEY(meal_id) REFERENCES meals(id)) STRICT')
while True:
    line = input('> ').strip()
    if line == 'quit':
        break
    if ':' in line:
        meal, _, rest = line.partition(':')
        meal = meal.strip()
        items = [item.strip() for item in rest.split(',') if item.strip()]
        conn.execute('BEGIN')
        try:
            meal_id = conn.execute('INSERT INTO meals (name) VALUES (?)', [meal]).lastrowid
            conn.executemany('INSERT INTO ingredients (name, meal_id) VALUES (?, ?)', [(item, meal_id) for item in items])
            conn.execute('COMMIT')
            print('Meal added:', meal)
        except sqlite3.IntegrityError as error:
            conn.execute('ROLLBACK')
            print('Not added:', error)
        continue
    found = conn.execute('SELECT ingredients.name FROM ingredients JOIN meals ON meals.id = ingredients.meal_id WHERE meals.name = ? ORDER BY ingredients.rowid', [line]).fetchall()
    if found:
        print('Ingredients of ' + line + ':')
        for (item,) in found:
            print('  ' + item)
    used = conn.execute('SELECT meals.name FROM meals JOIN ingredients ON meals.id = ingredients.meal_id WHERE ingredients.name = ? ORDER BY meals.id', [line]).fetchall()
    if used:
        print('Meals that use ' + line + ':')
        for (name,) in used:
            print('  ' + name)
    if not found and not used:
        print('Nothing known about ' + line)
conn.close()

findings: Background

Chapter 16 of the 3rd edition, SQLite Databases, sets a database against the spreadsheets of chapters 14 and 15 and SQLite against server databases; creates a database and a table with sqlite3.connect(), isolation_level=None and CREATE TABLE ... STRICT, names the data types, reads sqlite_schema and PRAGMA TABLE_INFO; teaches CRUD with INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE, the ? placeholder against SQL injection, fetchall() and iteration, WHERE, LIKE and GLOB, ORDER BY, LIMIT and CREATE INDEX; BEGIN with commit() and rollback() and the ACID properties; backup(); ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE; foreign keys and the inner join; in-memory databases; iterdump(); the sqlite3 shell and three graphical applications; and ends with practice questions and two practice programs, the Cat Vaccination Checker and the Meal Ingredients Database. The chapter page of 2026-10-12 is 113,075 bytes with 49 listings (44 of them interactive sessions of 131 statements), 3 captioned figures and 1 table, and its sha256, b861ab3300b167a8ecb9c5882052315f3362cc74477f647462eb6d198b5b39a4, equals the chapterDigest of the book's own chapter ontology [P01] [P03] [P04] [P05].
Background

The ideas the chapter borrows have a history the page leaves out. Codd's 1970 paper introduced the relational model, IBM's heritage page tells the story of the relational database, SQLite was written by D. Richard Hipp and is public domain, is described by its authors as the most widely deployed database engine, is tested with simulated power loss, and is serverless; the largest database is 281 terabytes (the executed maximum page count times the page size gave 281,474,976,579,584 bytes). Practical SQL (DeBarros, 2022) is the book the chapter points to for further SQL [P05] [P22] [P23] [P24] [P35] [P36] [P44] [P67] [P68] [P69] [P70] [P71] [P72] [P73] [P74].
Comparative analysis

The chapter's interactive sessions were replayed statement by statement, in order, on the shipped sweigartcats.db under Python 3.14.6 with SQLite 3.53.1: of 131 statements 103 printed what the page prints, 27 differ and 1 is a placeholder (sqlite3.sqlite_version, printed as 3.xx.xx by the page, gave 3.53.1). The differences are of two kinds. The data differ: the page's LIKE queries print rowids such as (5, 'Toby') and (49, 'Java') where the shipped file has (11, 'Toby') and (55, 'Java'), and the page prints one Zophie where the replay returns three. The other differences are listed one by one in the third-party record [P01] [P02] [P06].
Comparative analysis

The foreign key of the chapter's second table cannot be enforced. The shipped vaccinations table declares FOREIGN KEY(cat_id) REFERENCES cats(rowid), and the cats table has no column named rowid and no primary key, so with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON every INSERT into vaccinations fails with foreign key mismatch - 'vaccinations' referencing 'cats', identically under Python 3.14.0 to 3.14.6, 3.13 and 3.12 and the SQLite libraries 3.45.1, 3.50.4 and 3.53.1. SQLite's foreign key page requires the parent key to be the primary key or a column with a UNIQUE index, and rowid is neither unless it is an alias. A table rebuilt with id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and REFERENCES cats(id) enforced the constraint and reported the orphan with PRAGMA foreign_key_check. The chapter's join works because a join does not need the constraint [P01] [P02] [P11] [P18].
Comparative analysis

Connection.iterdump() fails on the book's own database from Python 3.13: the implementation runs PRAGMA foreign_key_check first, and on the shipped file that raises OperationalError: foreign key mismatch, so the chapter's dump example cannot be run on the file the book ships (Python 3.12 and 3.11 return 395 lines of the same file).  [P06] [P54] [P21].
Comparative analysis

The chapter says SQLite has six data types and lists five. A STRICT table accepts the type names INT, INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB and ANY, which is six words; the storage classes are five (NULL, INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB); and the names the chapter's own lists use, BOOLEAN, DATE, VARCHAR, NUMERIC and FLOAT, are refused in a STRICT table and have only an affinity in an ordinary one. The statement that STRICT came with release 3.37.0, used by Python 3.11 and later, is right for the release (2021-11-27) and was run on 3.11.17, which links 3.45.1 [P01] [P08] [P09] [P47].
Comparative analysis

A STRICT table checks the type of what is stored, not what is bound: the text 'Hello' and the real 3.5 are refused in an INTEGER column ('cannot store TEXT value in INTEGER column'), the text '42' is converted to the integer 42, 42.0 is stored as 42, and a column with no type is a syntax error (missing datatype). SQLite has no boolean and no date type: True is stored as 1, and dates are text, real or integer read by the date functions, with Python's default date adapter deprecated since 3.12 (DeprecationWarning, run under all interpreters from 3.12) [P08] [P09] [P38] [P55].
Comparative analysis

The chapter's double-quoted text in queries (WHERE name LIKE 'Ja%') works only because SQLite accepts a double-quoted string that matches no column. fur = 'fur' compared the column with itself and returned all 4 rows, and the build's compile options list no DQS setting, so the legacy behaviour is on. SQLite's own page on quirks lists 'Double-quoted String Literals Are Accepted' among its gotchas and its compile-time options call the behaviour a misfeature that SQLITE_DQS=0 disables. The expressions page adds that LIKE understands upper and lower case only for ASCII characters by default [P01] [P12] [P13] [P34].
Comparative analysis

An index serves a search but not every search the chapter makes. On 300,000 rows a search by indexed name took 0.0033 ms against 10.27 ms for a scan (a ratio of 3,087 on one run) and 300,000 inserts took 4.7 times as long with two indexes (0.56 s against 0.12 s); the query plan showed SEARCH ... USING INDEX for name = 'Mango', for GLOB 'Ma*' and for a range, but SCAN cats for LIKE 'Ma%' and for LIKE '%ango', because the default index uses the BINARY collation and LIKE is case-insensitive. The chapter's LIKE queries would not use the index it builds. The timings are labelled MEASURED in the record and vary with the machine [P01] [P30] [P31] [P32].
Comparative analysis

The chapter says a database in memory is much faster than one in a file. With the default autocommit, 2,000 single inserts took 0.002 s in memory and 2.236 s in a file (every insert is a durable commit); when the same inserts ran in one transaction the file took 0.0025 s against 0.0011 s. Speed is decided by the commit, not by the place. Each connect(':memory:') is a separate database, a URI with mode=memory and cache=shared is visible to two connections, and connect('') gave a private database with an empty file name [P01] [P19] [P51] [P15].
Comparative analysis

The chapter's warning about hundreds or thousands of simultaneous writers was tried: 100 and then 1,000 operating-system processes each inserted 5 rows into one file. Under the rollback journal 1,000 writers stored 5,000 rows with no error in 52.6 s, and under write-ahead logging the same took 4.24 s (100 writers: 1.80 s and 0.83 s). Nothing was lost because each writer waits up to the module's 5-second default timeout; a writer that holds a lock longer gets 'database is locked'. So the limit is throughput, not correctness, and WAL helps readers and writers. The 1,000-process experiment is one run on one machine [P01] [P20] [P22] [P27].
Comparative analysis

The chapter's statement that the rowid does not change when other rows are deleted holds for the rows that stay but not for the number. After deleting the row with the largest rowid, the next insert received that same rowid again (4, then 5); VACUUM renumbered the rowids of a table that has no INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (3 and 4 became 1 and 2); and a column declared INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is an alias of the rowid and keeps its value, while AUTOINCREMENT adds a table that stops reuse.  The chapter's foreign key points at the rowid, which is the number VACUUM may change [P01] [P10] [P16] [P17] [P18].
Comparative analysis

The injection example of the chapter is sound and understated. An f-string with x' OR '1'='1 returned all 4 rows where the bound parameter returned none, and execute() refused a second statement ('You can only execute one statement at a time'), so the xkcd 327 attack does not drop a table through execute(), though executescript() would. OWASP and MITRE name the weakness (CWE-89) and recommend parameterised queries; the strangers the chapter mentions include a file, a form or a spreadsheet of an earlier chapter. [P01] [P64] [P65] [P66] [P75].
Comparative analysis

The shipped database holds planted errors that the chapter's practice program is meant to find: 3 vaccinations dated before the birth of the cat (Ruby, Java, Rocket), 7 cats missing at least one of the three vaccines (Molly, Sage, Hugh, Chester, Snowflake, Luke, Muffin), no orphan vaccination rows, 97 vaccinations of each vaccine and two cats named Tiger. The file is 24,576 bytes with 100 cats and 291 vaccinations, and it is identical in sha256 (41f0d0b5bc2e...) to the file the online-materials zip also ships as sweigartcats-original.db. The zip itself is not kept in the repository; the scripts fetch it and check the hash [P02] [P01].
Conclusion

An advanced course on chapter 16 should keep the chapter's CRUD and transaction teaching and correct or add: single quotes for text; the autocommit attribute instead of isolation_level=None; INTEGER PRIMARY KEY with a real foreign key, switched on with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON per connection; the BINARY index and LIKE; WAL and the busy timeout for several writers; one transaction for bulk inserts; closing connections with contextlib.closing; and running every listing against the file the book ships, with the dump limitation in mind. What could not be run (the graphical applications, Windows and macOS installs, apt) is listed as NOT EXECUTED where it comes up [P01] [P06] [P11] [P20] [P59] [P60].
Contemporary developments

The module's transaction control has two models. The chapter uses isolation_level=None, the legacy switch for autocommit; since Python 3.12 the connection has an autocommit attribute (absent on 3.11.17) that supersedes it. With autocommit=True, a rollback() after an INSERT leaves the row (1 row remained under every interpreter from 3.12), with autocommit=False the module opens a transaction itself, and execute('BEGIN') in that mode fails with 'cannot start a transaction within a transaction'. The default isolation_level is the empty string, which opens a transaction before an INSERT but not before CREATE TABLE. The Python 3.14 documentation calls autocommit=False the recommended value [P06] [P55] [P15].
Contemporary developments

The module's names and signatures moved under the chapter. sqlite3.version and sqlite3.version_info of the module are gone in Python 3.14 (AttributeError: module 'sqlite3' has no attribute 'version'); connect() with more than its first argument positional gives a DeprecationWarning from Python 3.13; a named placeholder given a sequence is an error from 3.14 where 3.13 and 3.12 warned; and a connection that is not closed raises a ResourceWarning when collected. The binary running on 2026-10-12 links SQLite 3.53.1 under Python 3.14.5 and 3.14.6 and 3.50.4 under 3.14.0 to 3.14.4, while sqlite.org offers release 3.54.0 (2026-10-09) [P06] [P48] [P53] [P54].
Contemporary developments

The sqlite3 shell and the graphical tools have changed in ways the page does not show. The official 3.54.0 shell, downloaded and checked against the SHA3-256 on the download page, prints a boxed table in a terminal and shows the prompt 'SQLite-3.54 example.db->', where the page prints the list mode. python -m sqlite3 is a second shell. SQLiteStudio's address https://sqlitestudio.pl answered 301 and its page is titled Letos; DB Browser for SQLite and DBeaver Community answered 200. The three applications were not installed and not run, and sudo apt install sqlite3 and the Windows and macOS installers were NOT EXECUTED [P01] [P21] [P49] [P61] [P62] [P63].

nodes.label: Database idea
nodes.body: Chapter 16 opens by setting a database against two things the reader already knows, the spreadsheet of chapters 14 and 15 and the plain text file, and against the other SQL databases the reader may have met (Sweigart, 2025). It calls SQLite a lightweight database included with Python, stored in a single file, and the most widely deployed database software (Sweigart, 2025)(SQLite documentation, 2026).

paras.text: Chapter 16 opens by setting a database against two things the reader already knows, the spreadsheet of chapters 14 and 15 and the plain text file, and against the other SQL databases the reader may have met (Sweigart, 2025). It calls SQLite a lightweight database included with Python, stored in a single file, and the most widely deployed database software (Sweigart, 2025)(SQLite documentation, 2026).

Three ideas carry this subject. Spreadsheet versus table covers the rowid, the one thing a table has that a sheet does not. SQLite versus servers covers the single file, the missing user roles and the real limits on size. Files versus database covers what a query does that a Python loop over a list does as well. Everything below was run on the shipped sweigartcats.db or on a table built to match it (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Spreadsheet versus table
nodes.body: The chapter says a table can be thought of as a spreadsheet, a list of tuples whose rows are records and whose columns are the kinds of data, and that SQLite adds a rowid column to each table, a unique integer that does not change when other rows are deleted (Sweigart, 2025). The SQLite pages on rowid tables and on VACUUM and AUTOINCREMENT qualify that last claim (SQLite documentation, 2026).

paras.text: The chapter says a table can be thought of as a spreadsheet, a list of tuples whose rows are records and whose columns are the kinds of data, and that SQLite adds a rowid column to each table, a unique integer that does not change when other rows are deleted (Sweigart, 2025). The SQLite pages on rowid tables and on VACUUM and AUTOINCREMENT qualify that last claim (SQLite documentation, 2026).

Five ideas follow. The table is a list of tuples. The rowid is hidden from SELECT star. A rowid can be handed out again. VACUUM can renumber rowids. A column declared INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is the stable alternative (This study, 2026). The claim that a primary key 'doesn't change' is true for the rows that stay and false for the number itself in these cases.

nodes.label: Table is tuple list
nodes.body: The chapter writes that the cats table is essentially [('Zophie', '2021-01-24', 'black', 5.6), ('Colin', '2016-12-24', 'siamese', 6.2), ...] (Sweigart, 2025). The DB-API says a fetch returns a sequence of rows, and the module's default row is a tuple (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Rowid reuse
nodes.body: The chapter says a record's primary key ID is unique and does not change, so that a cat keeps its identity through deletions and reordering (Sweigart, 2025). SQLite's page on AUTOINCREMENT says that without the keyword the automatic assignment may reuse the rowids of rows that were deleted, and that the keyword exists to prevent exactly that (SQLite documentation, 2026).

paras.text: The chapter says a record's primary key ID is unique and does not change, so that a cat keeps its identity through deletions and reordering (Sweigart, 2025). SQLite's page on AUTOINCREMENT says that without the keyword the automatic assignment may reuse the rowids of rows that were deleted, and that the keyword exists to prevent exactly that (SQLite documentation, 2026).

Deleting the row with the largest rowid and inserting a new row gave the new row that rowid; deleting a row in the middle did not free its number, because a new row takes one more than the largest in use (This study, 2026). A program that stores a rowid elsewhere after deleting the last row can therefore point at a different cat.

nodes.example: DELETE FROM cats WHERE rowid = 4; INSERT INTO cats ...
nodes.definition: A rowid freed by deleting the largest row is handed out again: after deleting rowid 4 the next insert received 4, and after deleting rowid 2 the next received 5, leaving rowids 1, 3, 4 and 5.

nodes.body: The chapter says sqlite3.connect() takes a filename or a pathlib.Path, creates an empty database when the file does not exist, raises sqlite3.DatabaseError: file is not a database at the first query if the file is something else, and returns a Connection that the program closes with conn.close() or leaves to be closed at exit (Sweigart, 2025). The Python documentation adds that since 3.13 a Connection deleted without close() emits a ResourceWarning (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The Python documentation says the connection used as a context manager commits or rolls back and does not close, recommends contextlib.closing for closing, and says that since 3.13 a ResourceWarning is emitted if close() is not called before the object is deleted (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Typing rules
nodes.body: The chapter says SQLite has data types, but is not strict about them: it stores 'Hello' in an INTEGER column, converts '42' to 42 by type affinity, and offers the STRICT keyword to enforce types, which it recommends; it also says there is no Boolean and no date type, so Booleans are INTEGER 0 and 1 and dates are TEXT in the formats of Table 16-1 (Sweigart, 2025). SQLite's page on datatypes says its dynamic typing associates the type with the value and not with the column (SQLite documentation, 2026).

Six ideas follow. Storage classes are what a value is. The chapter's six types are five storage classes and a miscount. Affinity is the conversion a column does. STRICT is the check a column does. Booleans and dates have conventions and no types. And Python values map onto storage classes by a fixed table (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Type affinity
nodes.body: The chapter says SQLite casts data to the column's type if possible, a feature called type affinity, and that 'Hello' in an INTEGER column is stored as 'Hello' without error (Sweigart, 2025). SQLite's page on datatypes gives five affinities, TEXT, NUMERIC, INTEGER, REAL and BLOB, and the rules by which the declared type of a column picks one (SQLite documentation, 2026).

nodes.definition: In an ordinary table the column type is a preference: '42' in an INTEGER column became the integer 42, 42 in a TEXT column became the text '42', '3.5' in a REAL column became 3.5, '7' in a NUMERIC column became the integer 7, and 'Hello' in an INTEGER column stayed the text 'Hello'.

nodes.body: The chapter creates a table with CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, lists the tables by selecting from sqlite_schema and lists the columns with PRAGMA TABLE_INFO(cats), and explains the six fields of each tuple (Sweigart, 2025). SQLite's pages on CREATE TABLE and on PRAGMA statements describe them, and the file format page lists sqlite_master as an alias of sqlite_schema (SQLite documentation, 2026).

nodes.label: Transaction control
nodes.body: A transaction is, in the chapter's words, a unit of work in a database; an INSERT begins one, and a program can run BEGIN and then undo everything with conn.rollback() or keep it with conn.commit() (Sweigart, 2025). The chapter adds the ACID test, that transactions are atomic, consistent, isolated and durable, and says SQLite is ACID-compliant and has passed tests that simulate losing power (Sweigart, 2025)(SQLite documentation, 2026).

The chapter adds the ACID test, that transactions are atomic, consistent, isolated and durable, and says SQLite is ACID-compliant and has passed tests that simulate losing power (Sweigart, 2025)(SQLite documentation, 2026).

Three ideas carry this subject. Boundaries covers where a transaction starts and ends under the three transaction-control modes of Python 3.14, and what the chapter's pattern does in each. Guarantees covers the four letters of ACID, each run once. Concurrency covers the lock that a second writer meets and the journal mode that changes it. The central finding is that the chapter's rollback pattern holds in the mode it uses and silently fails in the mode that the current documentation recommends (This study, 2026).

nodes.body: The chapter connects with isolation_level=None, which it says is autocommit mode that relieves the reader of calling commit() after each execute(), and then starts a transaction by hand with the query BEGIN, ending it with commit() or rollback() (Sweigart, 2025). The Python documentation describes three modes: the legacy one controlled by isolation_level, the autocommit attribute added in 3.12 and the PEP 249 behaviour with autocommit False (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Memory
nodes.body: The chapter says an in-memory database, opened with the filename ':memory:', makes a large number of queries much faster, that it must be saved with backup() and is lost if the program crashes, and that the same method loads a file into memory; the same method also backs up a database that other programs are using, where copying the file would not be safe (Sweigart, 2025). SQLite's pages on in-memory databases and the backup API describe both (SQLite documentation, 2026).

Two ideas follow. An in-memory database belongs to its connection, and a second connection to ':memory:' is a different empty database. And backup() copies whole databases in either direction, in steps if asked, and replaces the content of its target (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: In memory database
nodes.body: The chapter says to pass ':memory:' as the filename for an in-memory database and warns that it is lost if the program crashes (Sweigart, 2025). SQLite's page on in-memory databases says each connection to ':memory:' creates a new database, that a named in-memory database can be shared with the URI file:memdb1?mode=memory&cache=shared, and that an empty filename gives a temporary database (SQLite documentation, 2026).

The chapter's claim that memory databases are significantly faster is measured in the third-party record, where inserts into memory and into a file are compared; with autocommit and a journal on disk the file is the slow one, and in one transaction the difference shrinks.

nodes.label: Backup method
nodes.body: The chapter says backup() safely backs up a database in between the other queries being run on it, that shutil.copy of the file is enough when no program uses the database, and shows file to file, memory to file and file to memory (Sweigart, 2025). The Python documentation says backup works even if the database is being accessed by other clients, takes pages, progress and sleep arguments, and was added in 3.7 (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The practice question 16 asks how to copy a database to another database.

nodes.label: Dump
nodes.body: The chapter says iterdump() returns an iterator of the SQL statements that re-create a database, writes it to sweigartcats-queries.txt line by line and prints a listing that starts with BEGIN TRANSACTION and ends with COMMIT, with the table name in double quotes, and says the text is almost certainly larger than the database (Sweigart, 2025). The Python documentation adds a filter argument in 3.13 (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Two ideas follow. On an ordinary table the dump is a script that rebuilds the same rows. And on the shipped file the chapter's own example fails under Python 3.13 and 3.14, because the dump routine checks the foreign keys first and the chapter's key is the one that SQLite cannot use (This study, 2026).

lecture.title: Chapter 16: SQLite Databases
lecture.say: Chapters 14 and 15 worked on spreadsheets: a file that a program opens from its own disk, and a sheet that lives on Google's servers. Chapter 16 turns to the tool that replaces both when the data has to be searched, changed by several statements at once and kept consistent, a database, and to the one database that needs no server at all, SQLite. This deck follows the chapter in its own order: what a database table is and how it differs from a spreadsheet; how a program connects to a file and creates a table with types; the four operations of create, read, update and delete, with placeholders instead of pasted text; transactions that keep or undo a group of changes; the structure of tables, with foreign keys and joins; and copies, tools and the two practice programs. It adds what the chapter leaves out and what the research found when every printed output was run again: the foreign key of the chapter's second table cannot be enforced, the dump of the book's own database fails from Python 3.13, the number of data types is miscounted, a rowid can be handed out twice, and a database in memory is not the fast one. Everything printed on these slides was produced by Python 3.14.6, installed with uv, whose sqlite3 module links SQLite 3.53.1, and nothing needed a network except the two programs that fetch the book's database and check its hash.

lecture.title: Today's route
lecture.say: The route has seven parts. It starts with the idea of a database, what a program can do with SQLite, the beginning of SQLite and the way a table is a list of tuples with a hidden rowid, then the connection, the types, the schema and the values that go in, then the four operations with placeholders, the traps of a WHERE clause and the index, then transactions and the two writers of one file, then the rowid, the foreign key that works and the one in the book that cannot be enforced, then copies, the first practice program and the tools, ending with a one-map summary and the resources. The ranges name the exact slides, so you can return to the part you need. Two of the slides are true stories and four more are told in the notes; the eight narrative diagrams of the chapter are drawn from the same specifications as the interactive page. Every output was printed by Python 3.14.6 with SQLite 3.53.1, the programs that read the book's database say so, and what could not be run is marked on its slide.

lecture.title: The questions this chapter answers
lecture.say: The first question is the chapter's spine, and it is a question about words. INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE change a database; SELECT only reads it; CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE change its structure. What decides whether a change is kept, undone or refused is the transaction: a statement that breaks a rule, such as a NOT NULL column or a STRICT type, is refused and leaves nothing behind, a group of statements is kept by commit() and undone by rollback(), and the module itself has two ways of deciding when a transaction begins. The second question is the watch-out of the deck. The chapter is sound in outline, but when its 131 interactive statements were replayed on the book's own database, 103 printed what the page prints, 27 differed and one was a placeholder; and several claims do not hold for the module or the library of today: the foreign key of the second table cannot be enforced, the dump of the shipped file fails from Python 3.13, the count of six data types lists five, and the index does not serve the chapter's own LIKE queries. Each slide says where a printed line differs and on what evidence. The chips give the size of the chapter as this deck covers it: six branches, the topics beneath them, the console rows and the programs that were run, the eight diagrams, and the Python and SQLite releases that printed every result.

lecture.title: SQLite and what a program can do with it
lecture.say: SQLite is not a server that a program talks to; it is a library that the program loads, and the database is one ordinary file. Because there is no server there are also no accounts to manage, and the console shows it: GRANT and CREATE USER are syntax errors. The same console shows how large such a file may grow. The default page is 4096 bytes and the default maximum is 4,294,967,294 pages, which is 17,592,186,036,224 bytes at that page size; at the largest page of 65,536 bytes the limit is 281,474,976,579,584 bytes, the 281 terabytes that SQLite's page on limits gives. The module is part of the Python standard library since release 2.5 of 19 September 2006, when the pysqlite wrapper was added under the name sqlite3. The library inside it belongs to the build, not to the language: the ten interpreters of the study, Python 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 and the seven releases 3.14.0 to 3.14.6, link SQLite 3.45.1, 3.50.4 or 3.53.1, and sqlite.org offered release 3.54.0 on 12 October 2026. SQLite is in the public domain, its authors describe it as the most widely deployed database engine, and it is tested with simulated power loss. The use-case diagram lists what a program can do with one database through the module: insert rows, read them with a query, update and delete them, alter and drop tables, join tables through a foreign key, and back a database up or dump it as text. The rest of the deck takes these in the order of the chapter.

lecture.title: SQLite began in 2000 on a Navy program
lecture.say: Wikipedia's history of SQLite says D. Richard Hipp designed it in the spring of 2000 while he worked for General Dynamics on a contract with the United States Navy. He was writing software for the damage-control system aboard guided-missile destroyers, a system that first used HP-UX with an Informix database as its back end. The article dates the first release of SQLite to 17 August 2000 and calls the software public domain. A database that is one file with no server to start, and no user accounts to grant, is the SQLite that chapter 16 opens with Python. The account rests on these sources. Wikipedia, 'SQLite' (History: designed in the spring of 2000 by D. Richard Hipp at General Dynamics for the US Navy; initial release 2000-08-17; public domain), read 2026-10-12; sqlite.org/about.html and sqlite.org/serverless.html. Two of the facts on the slide were also read on SQLite's own pages: that the code is in the public domain, and that a database is a single file read and written through a library.

lecture.title: Rows are tuples, and every row has a rowid
lecture.say: The chapter sets a table against a spreadsheet: a row is a record, a column has a name and a type, and SQLite adds a column of its own, the rowid, a whole number that identifies the row. The console builds the chapter's cats table with the keyword STRICT, which the next slides explain, stores two cats and reads them back. What comes back is a list, and each item of the list is a tuple, the first being ('Zophie', '2021-01-24', 'black', 5.6); that is the chapter's picture of a table as a list of tuples, and it holds. The rowid is hidden: SELECT * lists the four columns, SELECT rowid, * puts the rowid first, and rowid, oid and _rowid_ are three names for the same value. The helper do() runs a statement that returns no rows and prints nothing, and run() returns the rows of a statement, so the console prints only what matters; run it in any Python, because it uses a database in memory and the standard library alone. The chapter claims the rowid does not change when other rows are deleted, which is true of the rows that stay but not of the number itself; slide 19 shows when it is handed out again. The chapter's opening question, the cats between 3 and 5 kilograms born before October 2023, was also run on the book's database: the query and a Python loop over all 100 rows returned the same six cats.

lecture.title: From connect() to rows, and a closed file
lecture.say: This is the chapter's own sequence of steps, drawn as a workflow: connect to a database file, create the table if it does not exist, insert the rows, commit if the statement changed the data, read the rows with fetchall, and close the connection. The console runs the ends of it on a database in memory. A connection starts outside a transaction, SELECT sqlite_version() returns the library's release, 3.53.1 here, and after close() any statement raises ProgrammingError: Cannot operate on a closed database. A few more facts come from the study. connect() creates the file at once but writes nothing: a new example.db was 0 bytes after connect and after a SELECT, and 8,192 bytes after the first CREATE TABLE. A text file connects without an error and fails at the first statement with file is not a database. A with block commits or rolls back but does not close the connection; closing() from contextlib does, and a connection that is simply dropped raises a ResourceWarning. The chapter says a database in memory is much faster than one in a file, and the card gives the measurement behind the correction. The numbers are one run on one machine on 12 October 2026 and vary with the machine, and what they show is that speed is decided by the commit, not by the place. Each connect(':memory:') is a separate database, so two connections to memory do not see each other's tables. The story of the module is short: Python 2.5, released on 19 September 2006, added the pysqlite wrapper to the standard library as sqlite3, which is why a program can open a database with no installation.

lecture.title: STRICT, affinity and the six that are five
lecture.say: The program makes two tables with an INTEGER column, one STRICT and one ordinary, and tries to insert five values into each: the text 'Hello', the real 3.5, the text '42', the real 42.0 and NULL. In the STRICT table 'Hello' and 3.5 are refused with IntegrityError, cannot store TEXT value in INTEGER column s.i, and cannot store REAL value in INTEGER column; '42' is converted to the integer 42, 42.0 is stored as 42, and NULL is stored. In the ordinary table all five go in, because the declared type is only an affinity, a preference: '42' became the integer 42, 42.0 became 42, but 'Hello' stayed text and 3.5 stayed real, which typeof() shows. The last statement tries a column of type BOOLEAN in a STRICT table and gets OperationalError, unknown datatype for bad.a. The chapter's own count is off by one: it says that SQLite has six data types and lists five, and the five it lists are the storage classes NULL, INTEGER, REAL, TEXT and BLOB. A STRICT table accepts the six type words INT, INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB and ANY, and the names the chapter's lists use, such as BOOLEAN, DATE, VARCHAR, NUMERIC and FLOAT, are refused in a STRICT table and only have an affinity in an ordinary one. The chapter's claim that STRICT came with a SQLite version used by Python 3.11 and later is right: the release log of SQLite 3.37.0 is dated 27 November 2021, and Python 3.11 was run with SQLite 3.45.1. The release log opens with STRICT tables as a prescriptive style of data type management for developers who prefer that kind of thing.

lecture.title: Reading the schema
lecture.say: The first listing of the chapter runs from top to bottom without a surprise, and the transcript is what it printed. connect() with isolation_level=None opens the file example.db, which the chapter treats as autocommit; CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS makes the STRICT table of cats; the query on sqlite_schema, where the type is a table, lists [('cats',)]; PRAGMA table_info(cats) returns one tuple for each column with the fields cid, name, type, notnull, dflt_value and pk, so the name column shows notnull 1; and the second CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, with a different column list, does nothing, because the table exists, so the stored SQL is still the first one. Without the words IF NOT EXISTS the same statement raises OperationalError, table cats already exists, for cats and for CATS alike, because table names are not case-sensitive. sqlite_schema lists tables, indexes and views in the order they were created, and sqlite_master returned the same rows under the name that older programs use. The default value of a text column comes back as SQL text with its quotes, so a default of x is shown as 'x'. Finally the program asks whether the file has a size above zero, which is True because the CREATE TABLE has written the first pages; the study measured 8,192 bytes, two pages of 4,096 bytes, and the file was the only file left in the directory after the connection closed.

lecture.title: Python values and the five storage classes
lecture.say: The table is computed, not typed: for each Python value the program stores it in a column with no type, asks typeof() for the storage class SQLite chose and reads the value back to see which Python type returns. None becomes null and comes back as None, an int becomes integer, a float real, a str text and bytes a blob; True is stored as the integer 1 and comes back as an int, because SQLite has no boolean. The module binds exactly these five Python types and the boolean; a value of any other type is refused. The console shows two of the refusals: an int of 2 to the power 63 is too large for the 64 bits of an INTEGER and raises OverflowError, Python int too large to convert to SQLite INTEGER, and a list raises ProgrammingError, because the module cannot bind it. Dates have no type either. They are stored as text, as a real number or as an integer and read by the date functions, and the functions are forgiving in odd ways: date('31/10/2035') returns None, but date('2035-02-30') returns the invented date 2035-03-02. Python's default adapter for datetime.date objects is deprecated since Python 3.12 and warns under every interpreter from 3.12, so a program should write the text of the date itself. TRUE and FALSE are accepted in SQL and are 1 and 0.

lecture.title: Create, read, update and delete
lecture.say: Before this excerpt the program builds the cats table in memory and inserts four cats with executemany, one call for four rows. The excerpt then shows each operation with its answer. SELECT with ORDER BY and LIMIT 2 returns the two heaviest cats as (rowid, name); UPDATE with a question mark placeholder adds 0.1 to every black cat, and cur.rowcount is 2; DELETE ... WHERE name = ? RETURNING rowid, name deletes Jacob and hands back [(3, 'Jacob')] in one call; an INSERT of a name alone stores NULL in the other columns and lastrowid is 5; a SELECT with LIKE and ORDER BY lists the names with an o; and the last line aggregates: 4 rows, 3 with a fur, an average weight of 6.27. Look at the long number in the transcript: Toby's weight is shown as 6.8999999999999995 and Zophie's as 5.699999999999999, because 0.1 cannot be written exactly in binary floating point and SQLite's REAL is a double, so a program should round what it shows. The study also found how rowcount behaves: an UPDATE by rowid changed one row, the same UPDATE by name changed two cats named Zophie, UPDATE with a true condition changed all rows, DELETE with no condition removed every row and left the empty table in place. executemany is not all or nothing: when the second row of a second batch broke NOT NULL, the row before it stayed.

lecture.title: A placeholder keeps a value as data
lecture.say: A query with a question mark is an exchange in a fixed order. The program calls execute() with the statement and, as a separate tuple, the value; the module sends the statement and binds the value as data; SQLite returns the rows that match the whole value, and the module hands back a cursor. The console runs the attack. The text x' OR '1'='1 pasted into the query with an f-string closes the quote early and adds a condition that is always true, so every row comes back (both rows here, all four in the program of the next slide); the same text bound as a parameter is compared as one name and matches none. The third statement is the comic's attack: execute() refuses a second statement after a semicolon with ProgrammingError, You can only execute one statement at a time, so the table survives; executescript() runs several statements and would not refuse. OWASP and MITRE name the weakness, CWE-89, and recommend parameterised queries. The chapter's example is sound and, if anything, understated: the strangers whose text reaches a query include a file, a form or a spreadsheet read by an earlier chapter. A placeholder can stand for a value only, never for a table or column name. Named placeholders use a colon and a dictionary, and the errors are specific: a list given for :fur raises ProgrammingError, because a named parameter needs a mapping, and a dictionary without the key says You did not supply a value for binding parameter. A bare string such as 'black' is read as a sequence of five values.

lecture.title: Little Bobby Tables, 2007
lecture.say: xkcd number 327, 'Exploits of a Mom', was published on 10 October 2007. In it a school phones a mother about her son, whose name was written as text that closes a statement and drops the table of student records. The mother ends by hoping the school has learned to sanitize its database inputs. Chapter 16 answers the comic with the ? placeholder, and this study ran the attack: pasted into an f-string the text changed the query, bound as a parameter it matched nothing. The account rests on these sources. xkcd.com/327/ and xkcd.com/327/info.0.json (number 327, 2007-10-10, 'Exploits of a Mom', read 2026-10-12); this study's leaf SqlInjection. The transcript is the whole run of the chapter's injection program: four rows with the f-string, none with the placeholder, the refusal of the second statement, the table intact, and the three binding errors.

lecture.title: NULL, double quotes, LIKE and GLOB
lecture.say: The chapter filters with WHERE, and four details decide whether the filter does what the author means. NULL is not equal to anything, including NULL: fur = NULL matches no row, fur != 'black' skips the cat with no fur, because comparing NULL with anything gives NULL, which is not true, and IS NULL finds it; count(*) counts four rows where count(fur) counts three. The chapter writes its text in double quotes, as in WHERE name LIKE "Ja%", and that works only because SQLite accepts a double-quoted word that matches no column as a string. The study showed the other face of it: fur = "fur" compared the column with itself and matched every row with a fur, and the compile options of the build list no setting for it, so the legacy behaviour is on; SQLite's page on quirks lists double-quoted string literals among its gotchas, and the compile-time options call it a misfeature that SQLITE_DQS=0 disables. Use single quotes for text. Finally LIKE is case-insensitive for ASCII characters only by default, so 'a' LIKE 'A' is 1 but 'É' LIKE 'é' is 0, while GLOB is case-sensitive and uses * and ?. SQLite also accepts both = and == and both <> and !=, and BETWEEN is inclusive.

lecture.title: An index serves some searches, not all
lecture.say: The program builds a table of 1,000 cats, creates an index on the name and asks EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN for six searches. The plan says SEARCH ... USING INDEX idx_name for name = 'Cat0042', for name GLOB 'Cat00*' and for the range name >= 'Cat00' AND name < 'Cat01', and SCAN cats, a read of every row, for name LIKE 'Cat00%', for name LIKE '%42' and for fur = 'black', which has no index. LIKE does not use the index because the default index uses the BINARY collation and LIKE is case-insensitive, so the chapter's own LIKE queries would not use the index it builds; a leading wildcard could not use any ordinary index anyway. The last line counts the 100 names LIKE finds. An index is not free, and the chart shows the first price: the same 10,000 rows take 216 KiB in 54 pages of 4,096 bytes, 380 KiB with an index on the name and 512 KiB with a second index, each number computed again when the deck is checked. The card gives the other prices, in time, from the research record: a search by indexed name on 300,000 rows took 0.0033 ms against 10.27 ms for a scan, and 300,000 inserts took 4.7 times as long with two indexes. These are single runs on one machine and are not repeated by any check of the deck; the query plans and the sizes are.

lecture.title: Begin, then commit or roll back
lecture.say: The workflow is the chapter's section on rolling back transactions. BEGIN starts a transaction, the statements change the data, and one choice ends it: if every statement succeeded, commit() keeps the changes, and otherwise rollback() undoes them. The console runs it with isolation_level=None, the chapter's switch for autocommit, so nothing is inside a transaction until BEGIN. After BEGIN and one INSERT, in_transaction is True; rollback() leaves count(*) at 0; a second BEGIN with an INSERT and commit() keeps one row; and one INSERT of three rows, the last with NULL in a NOT NULL column, is refused as a whole, with IntegrityError, and the count is still 1, because a single statement is atomic. The study also found that DDL is part of a transaction: a CREATE TABLE and a DROP TABLE inside BEGIN were undone by rollback(), and a rollback() after a lone INSERT in this mode undid nothing, because the INSERT had already been committed. The ACID properties, atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability, were named by Theo Haerder and Andreas Reuter in their 1983 paper, Principles of Transaction-Oriented Database Recovery, in ACM Computing Surveys, building on earlier work of researchers including Jim Gray. SQLite's own pages describe it as transactional and test it with simulated power loss. In the study an open transaction was invisible to a second connection until commit(), and a committed row survived closing and reopening while an uncommitted one did not. Another feature is that executescript() commits any pending transaction first.

lecture.title: Three ways to begin a transaction
lecture.say: The module has two models of transaction control, and the transcript shows both. The first three lines come from a loop that opens a connection three times, with the default mode, with autocommit=False and with autocommit=True, creates a table, commits, inserts a row and calls rollback(). In the default mode, the legacy one, in_transaction is True after the INSERT but would stay False after a CREATE TABLE, and rollback() removes the row; with autocommit=False the module opens a transaction itself, rollback() removes the row and a new transaction opens at once; with autocommit=True the INSERT is committed immediately, in_transaction is False and rollback() leaves the row. The autocommit attribute exists from Python 3.12 on, it was absent on 3.11.17 and the 3.14 documentation calls autocommit=False the recommended value, so the chapter's isolation_level=None is the older switch. The excerpt then shows the context manager: a with block commits when it ends and rolls back when it raises, so the block that inserted 1 and then NULL left no rows, the transcript says NOT NULL constraint failed: t.a and rows after the failed block: 0. Finally one statement that inserts three rows, the last with NULL, is atomic and leaves none. In autocommit=False mode, execute('BEGIN') fails with cannot start a transaction within a transaction, because the module has opened one.

lecture.title: Two writers, one file
lecture.say: The chapter warns that SQLite is not the right choice for hundreds or thousands of simultaneous write operations, and the program tries the smallest case of it. Two connections open the same file with timeout 0. The first runs BEGIN IMMEDIATE and an INSERT and holds the write lock; the second asks to write at the same time and is answered with OperationalError, database is locked; in the default journal mode, delete, a reader sees 0 rows; the first commits and releases the lock. Then PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL switches the database to write-ahead logging, the first connection opens a write again and the second reads the committed count, 1, without being blocked; after the commit it reads 2. The directory then holds shared.db, shared.db-shm and shared.db-wal, and after both connections close only shared.db remains. The module's default busy timeout is 5 seconds, so a writer waits for the lock rather than failing at once, and only a writer that waits longer gets the error. The research tried the chapter's warning with 100 and then 1,000 operating-system processes that each inserted 5 rows into one file: nothing was lost, and the cost showed in time, so the limit is throughput and not correctness. Both numbers on the slide are one run on one machine on 12 October 2026 and vary with the machine.

lecture.title: The rowid is not a promise
lecture.say: The chapter says that the rowid does not change when other rows are deleted, and the state diagram follows one rowid to show where the sentence is too strong. A row is inserted and receives the next rowid. If the row is deleted and it was the one with the largest rowid, the next insert receives that same number again, 4 and then 5 on the table with AUTOINCREMENT in the transcript, where a plain table gave 4 twice. A table with no INTEGER PRIMARY KEY can have its rowids renumbered by VACUUM: after deleting rows 1 and 2 of four, the rows (3, 'c') and (4, 'e') became (1, 'c') and (2, 'e'). A column declared INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is an alias for the rowid and keeps its values through VACUUM, and with AUTOINCREMENT a deleted number is never handed out again, which costs the table sqlite_sequence, the only name beginning with sqlite_ in the last line of the transcript. Why this matters comes two slides on: the chapter's foreign key points at the rowid, the very number VACUUM may change. The first row and the transitions all come from the chapter's paragraph on the rowid and from SQLite's pages on rowid tables, VACUUM and AUTOINCREMENT, which the research read and ran.

lecture.title: A foreign key that works, and a join
lecture.say: This is the second practice program of the chapter, the meal ingredients database, made so that it works. The book specifies a table of meals with a name and a foreign key REFERENCES meals (rowid); as printed, the first INSERT into ingredients fails with foreign key mismatch, so the program here gives the parent table an id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and references meals (id), and switches enforcement on with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON, which is off by default and per connection. The first excerpt is the two CREATE TABLE statements, the second the checks: the join returns ('Pancakes', 'flour, milk, egg', 600.0) and ('Omelette', 'egg, butter', 170.0); an ingredient for meal 99 is refused with FOREIGN KEY constraint failed; PRAGMA foreign_key_check lists no orphans; and the meals that have no butter are [('Pancakes',)]. The program shown is the deck's copy of the corpus program with its SQL cut into pieces that fit a slide, and a check of the build requires that it print exactly what the corpus original prints. The idea behind the two tables is old. In June 1970 Edgar F. Codd, a mathematician at IBM's San Jose Research Lab, published A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks in Communications of the ACM, volume 13, number 6; IBM's history page tells how, before it, getting data out of the large information systems of the 1960s took specialists who often wrote whole programs to reach one fact. A table for each kind of fact, linked by a number and read back with a join, is the relational model in a few lines.

lecture.title: The book's foreign key cannot be enforced
lecture.say: The shipped database holds the cats table without a primary key and the vaccinations table with FOREIGN KEY(cat_id) REFERENCES cats(rowid), and that declaration cannot be enforced. SQLite's page on foreign keys requires the parent key to be the primary key or a column with a UNIQUE index, and rowid is neither unless it is an alias, so with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON every INSERT into vaccinations fails with OperationalError, foreign key mismatch - 'vaccinations' referencing 'cats', exactly as the transcript shows; it is off by default, which is why the book's examples seem to work. The identical result came from Python 3.14.0 to 3.14.6, 3.13 and 3.12, and from SQLite 3.45.1, 3.50.4 and 3.53.1. A table rebuilt with id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and REFERENCES cats(id) enforced the constraint and reported the orphan with PRAGMA foreign_key_check. The chapter's join works because a join does not need the constraint. The second finding follows from the first: Connection.iterdump() runs PRAGMA foreign_key_check first from Python 3.13, so on this file it raises the same OperationalError, while Python 3.12 and 3.11 return 395 lines of the same file. The file is the one the program fetches from the online materials of the third edition, 24,576 bytes with 4,096-byte pages, passing integrity_check, with 100 cats and 291 vaccinations; the zip also ships it a second time as sweigartcats-original.db, byte for byte equal. The deck's program is the corpus program with its long printed line cut in two.

lecture.title: Copy a database: backup() or iterdump()
lecture.say: The workflow has one real choice: is the copy to be a database or a text of SQL statements? A database copy is made with backup(), which copies the pages of one connection into another, and the program saves a database held in memory to the file copy.db, which then holds both rows in 8,192 bytes; backing up a connection onto itself raises ValueError, target cannot be the same connection instance. A text copy is made with iterdump(), which yields the statements of a database one at a time, and the transcript lists them: BEGIN TRANSACTION, the CREATE TABLE, one INSERT for each row, with the table name in double quotes, and COMMIT. Running them with executescript in an empty database rebuilt identical rows, and filter='cats' leaves out the index line. In the study backup() with pages=1 called its progress function several times and ended with status 101, SQLITE_DONE. The decision on the second branch is the finding of the research: on the book's own file iterdump() raises OperationalError, foreign key mismatch, from Python 3.13, because it runs PRAGMA foreign_key_check first, so the repair is to give the cats table a real key and dump again. The sqlite3 shell of release 3.54.0 has its own .dump command; the study ran it on a script and its dump began with PRAGMA foreign_keys=OFF.

lecture.title: The first practice program, and the tools
lecture.say: The first practice program of the chapter walks the book's own database and looks for the planted errors. The query joins vaccinations to cats and finds three vaccinations dated before the cat was born: Ruby, Java and Rocket, each with FVRCP and a date from 2001 to 2004 against a birth in 2013 to 2023. A second query, with a LEFT JOIN and a count of distinct vaccines, finds seven cats that lack at least one of the three vaccines, rabies, FeLV and FVRCP: Molly, Sage, Hugh, Chester, Snowflake, Luke and Muffin, none lacking all three. There are 97 vaccinations of each vaccine, no orphan rows, and two cats named Tiger, so the name cannot identify a cat. The program is the deck's copy of the corpus program, with the long queries cut and one result printed per line. The tools were checked in part. The sqlite3 shell of release 3.54.0 was downloaded from sqlite.org, its SHA3-256 checked against the download page, and run on a script and in a terminal, where it prints a boxed table and the prompt SQLite-3.54 example.db-> where the book shows the list mode. python -m sqlite3 is a second shell inside Python. The page of SQLiteStudio now answers with a redirect to a page titled Letos, and DB Browser for SQLite and DBeaver Community answered 200. The three applications were not installed, and the installers and sudo apt install sqlite3 were not run, so nothing on this slide is claimed about how they behave.

lecture.title: The chapter in one map
lecture.say: These six branches are the route of the deck. The idea of a database comes first: a table is like a spreadsheet with a rowid, SQLite is one file with no server, and a query replaces a loop over a list. Connection and schema follow: connect() opens or creates the file, a STRICT table checks the types and the schema is read from sqlite_schema. CRUD operations are the largest branch: insert, update and delete change the rows, a placeholder keeps a value as data and an index speeds up a search. Transactions keep or undo changes, and a failed statement changes nothing; write-ahead logging helps several writers. Table structure covers alter and drop, the foreign key that links two tables and the join that reads them together. The last branch is copies, tools and practice: backup() and iterdump() copy a database, the sqlite3 shell and three graphical applications, and two practice programs use the shipped file. Together they answer the first question of the chapter, which statements change the database and what keeps the change, and the slides that say where a printed line differs answer the second.

lecture.title: Where to go from here
lecture.say: Every link on this slide was opened on the day the deck was made, and the build records the status each answered. The textbook chapter is free to read online and holds every listing of the chapter, the Python documentation describes the sqlite3 module of release 3.14, and Practical SQL by Anthony DeBarros is the book the chapter points to for further SQL. The reference links are SQLite's own pages for the topics where the deck corrected the chapter: STRICT tables, foreign keys, transactions and write-ahead logging; the rest of the sixty-odd sources of the research, among them the pages on rowid tables, on VACUUM, on the query optimizer and on locking, are in the research package. The history links are the sources behind the six stories of the chapter. Two of them are slides, the beginning of SQLite and Little Bobby Tables; the other four were told in the notes: Codd's paper of 1970 on the slide of the meal ingredients, the arrival of sqlite3 in Python 2.5 on the slide of the connection, the strict mode of SQLite 3.37.0 on the slide of the types, and the name ACID of 1983 on the slide of the transaction.

lecture.title: What you should now be able to say
lecture.say: Four claims, each carried by a result you saw printed. If you can say them in your own words and run the examples yourself, you have the chapter. The console rows use only the standard library and a database in memory, so they can be typed into any Python, including one in a browser; the programs that build their own database need nothing else, and the two that read the book's file fetch it and check its hash first. The rows were run again under Python 3.14.6 with SQLite 3.53.1 each time the deck was built, and the programs were run again by the check that compares the slides with the recording. The next chapter of the book works with PDF and Word documents, where a program reads and writes files that other people made, and what this chapter taught about rows, types, keys and the cost of every commit carries over to any data that has to be kept in one place and kept correct.

import sqlite3

stories.title: SQLite was written in 2000 so that a Navy warship program no longer needed a database server
stories.who: D. Richard Hipp, then working for General Dynamics on a contract with the United States Navy
stories.where: Software for the damage-control system of guided-missile destroyers
stories.story: Wikipedia's history of SQLite says D. Richard Hipp designed it in the spring of 2000 while he worked for General Dynamics on a contract with the United States Navy. He was writing software for the damage-control system aboard guided-missile destroyers, a system that first used HP-UX with an Informix database as its back end. The article dates the first release of SQLite to 17 August 2000 and calls the software public domain. A database that is one file with no server to start, and no user accounts to grant, is the SQLite that chapter 16 opens with Python.
stories.lesson: A database can be a library and a file, not a server
stories.source: Wikipedia, 'SQLite' (History: designed in the spring of 2000 by D. Richard Hipp at General Dynamics for the US Navy; initial release 2000-08-17; public domain), read 2026-10-12; sqlite.org/about.html and sqlite.org/serverless.html.

stories.title: A 1970 paper from IBM's San Jose lab proposed the tables that a SQLite file still holds
stories.who: Edgar F. Codd, a mathematician at the IBM San Jose Research Lab
stories.where: Communications of the ACM, volume 13, number 6
stories.story: IBM's history page tells how Edgar F. Codd, an Oxford-educated mathematician at the IBM San Jose Research Lab, published a paper in 1970 titled 'A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks'. The paper is in Volume 13, Number 6 of Communications of the ACM, dated June 1970. Before it, IBM says, getting data out of the large information systems of the 1960s took specialists who often wrote whole programs to reach one fact. The chapter's cats table and vaccinations table, linked by a number and read back with a join, are the relational model in a few lines.
stories.lesson: Put each kind of fact in its own table and join them
stories.source: IBM, 'The relational database', ibm.com/history/relational-database (read 2026-10-12); E. F. Codd, 'A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks', Communications of the ACM 13(6), June 1970 (the paper's text, engineering.upenn.edu/~zives/03f/cis550/codd.pdf).

stories.title: Python 2.5 added the sqlite3 package to the standard library in 2006
stories.who: The Python developers, with the pysqlite module as the base
stories.story: What's New in Python 2.5, written by A.M. Kuchling, states that Python 2.5 was released on September 19, 2006. It lists the SQLite database module among the new modules, together with ElementTree and ctypes. The section on the package says the pysqlite wrapper had been added to the standard library under the name sqlite3. Since then a Python program can open a database file with no install, which is why chapter 16 can start with import sqlite3. The library inside it is a separate component, so the version of SQLite depends on the Python build.
stories.lesson: Python ships the module, the build decides the SQLite
stories.source: Python documentation, 'What's New in Python 2.5' (release date; the sqlite3 package section), docs.python.org/3.14/whatsnew/2.5.html, read 2026-10-12; this study's record of ten interpreters, which link SQLite 3.45.1, 3.50.4 and 3.53.1.

stories.title: A webcomic in 2007 made 'Little Bobby Tables' the standard warning about SQL injection
stories.who: Randall Munroe, the author of xkcd
stories.where: xkcd comic number 327, 'Exploits of a Mom'
stories.story: xkcd number 327, 'Exploits of a Mom', was published on 10 October 2007. In it a school phones a mother about her son, whose name was written as text that closes a statement and drops the table of student records. The mother ends by hoping the school has learned to sanitize its database inputs. Chapter 16 answers the comic with the ? placeholder, and this study ran the attack: pasted into an f-string the text changed the query, bound as a parameter it matched nothing.
stories.lesson: Bind values with placeholders; never paste them into SQL
stories.source: xkcd.com/327/ and xkcd.com/327/info.0.json (number 327, 2007-10-10, 'Exploits of a Mom', read 2026-10-12); this study's leaf SqlInjection.

stories.title: SQLite 3.37.0 gave tables a strict mode in November 2021
stories.story: The release log of SQLite 3.37.0 is dated 2021-11-27 and opens with STRICT tables, a prescriptive style of data type management for developers who prefer that kind of thing. Before that release a column's declared type was only a preference, so text could land in a column declared INTEGER. The chapter builds every table with STRICT, and in this study the text 'Hello' was refused in an INTEGER column of a strict table and stored as text in a plain one. Python 3.11 was run with SQLite 3.45.1, newer than the release that added the keyword.
stories.lesson: Declare STRICT so a column's type is a rule
stories.source: SQLite release log 3.37.0 (2021-11-27), sqlite.org/releaselog/3_37_0.html, read 2026-10-12; sqlite.org/stricttables.html; this study's leaves StrictMode and StrictVersionClaim.

stories.title: Two German researchers gave transactions the name ACID in 1983
stories.where: ACM Computing Surveys, in the paper 'Principles of Transaction-Oriented Database Recovery'
stories.story: Wikipedia says the acronym ACID appears in Theo Haerder and Andreas Reuter's 1983 paper, 'Principles of Transaction-Oriented Database Recovery', which built on earlier work on transactions by researchers including Jim Gray. The paper grouped atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability as the properties of a transaction. SQLite's own pages describe SQLite as transactional and test it with simulated power loss. In this study a failed statement changed nothing, and a committed row was still there when the file was opened again.
stories.lesson: A transaction is all of its changes or none
stories.source: Wikipedia, 'ACID' (the 1983 paper by Haerder and Reuter, ACM Computing Surveys), read 2026-10-12; sqlite.org/transactional.html and sqlite.org/testing.html; this study's leaves AtomicStatement and DurableAfterReopen.
